title: Short Research Projects
keyIdea: A short research project builds knowledge about one topic by looking at different parts of it. Plan a few research questions that facts can answer, each about a different aspect. Gather information from print and digital sources you can check: you can see who made them and when. Take brief notes in key words and your own words, without changing the facts. Sort the notes into categories that match your questions. Check important facts in a second source, and look further when sources disagree. Finish with a list of sources, giving the title and who made each one.

kid: A research project starts with a topic, like volcanoes. A topic is too big to answer in one go. So split it into questions. Where are volcanoes found? Why do they erupt? How do people know one is coming? Each question looks at a different part.

Next, find sources. Print sources are on paper, like an encyclopedia or an atlas. Digital sources are online, like a science website or a video by an expert. Use sources where you can see who made them and when. A post with no name, a made-up story or an advert is not one to trust for facts.

Take notes as you read. A note is a few key words in your own words, not the whole sentence copied out. Check that your note still says the same fact. If the source says most volcanoes, do not write all volcanoes.

Sort your notes under your questions, so each part of the topic has its own facts. Check big facts in two sources. If they disagree, look at a third trusted source. At the end, list your sources: the title and who made each one.
adult: This matches the Common Core writing standards for grades 4 and 5 (W.4.7, W.4.8, W.5.7, W.5.8). Pupils conduct short research projects that build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic. They gather relevant information from print and digital sources, take notes and categorize information, and provide a list of sources. In grade 5 they also summarize or paraphrase information in notes and finished work. In England the same skills sit in the Key Stage 2 programme: retrieve, record and present information from non-fiction, and note and develop ideas, drawing on reading and research.

The useful terms are research question, aspect, print source, digital source, reliable source, key words, notes, paraphrase (the same meaning in your own words), summarize (only the main points), categorize, cross-check and list of sources. A good research question is open and answerable from evidence. A feeling question, a yes/no question or a whole topic is not.

Common mistakes: asking about the whole topic, or asking opinion questions. Trusting the first page found, or thinking any book beats any website. Copying whole sentences, which is plagiarism and skips the thinking. Changing the meaning while shortening a note, so 'most' becomes 'all'. And writing 'the internet' or 'Google' as a source.

In the lab your child plans three questions about volcanoes and sees why an opinion, a yes/no question, 'everything' or a repeat is refused. They sort seven print and digital sources and pick the best of three notes, where the copy and the changed fact are both rejected. Then they file notes under headings and cross-check three facts in two sources.

familyTip: Pick a topic your child is curious about and ask them for three questions about different parts of it. When they find a fact online, ask: who made this page, and where else can we check it?

items: Note key words in your own words
Check a big fact in two sources
Use the first page you find

lab.caption: Flagship lab: plan three volcano questions, sort print and digital sources, make notes in your own words, file them by question and cross-check facts.

practice.prompt: Your topic is rainforests. Which is the best research question?
choices: Why do rainforests get so much rain?
practice.hint: Pick a question that facts can answer and that is small enough for a short project.
practice.explain: 'Why do rainforests get so much rain?' can be answered with facts. 'Nice' asks for an opinion, and 'everything' is the whole topic.

practice.prompt: You plan {q} research questions and want 2 sources for each one. How many sources is that, if none are shared?
practice.explain: {q} questions with 2 sources each make {=2*q} sources.

practice.prompt: The source says: 'Most bats hunt at night.' Which note keeps the fact right?
choices: bats only come out at night
practice.hint: Use key words, and do not change 'most' into something else.
practice.explain: 'most bats: hunt at night' is short and keeps 'most'. 'Only' changes the fact, and the last one is copied word for word.

practice.prompt: You have {a} notes under 'Where?' and {b} notes under 'Why?'. How many notes is that in all?
practice.hint: Add the notes in both categories.

pool.hint: Digital sources are found on a screen.
pool.explain: A website is a digital source. An encyclopedia and an atlas on paper are print sources.

pool.prompt: Why leave out a forum post with no name and no date?
choices: You cannot check who wrote it or if it is up to date
pool.hint: What do you need to know about a source to trust it?
pool.explain: Without a name or a date you cannot check the writer or whether the facts are current. Many websites are trustworthy when you can check who made them.

pool.prompt: What is wrong with copying a whole sentence into your notes?
choices: It is not in your own words, so it is not a note
pool.hint: What does a note look like?
pool.explain: A note is key words in your own words. Copying is not your work, and it skips the thinking that helps you understand.

pool.prompt: Two sources give different facts about the same thing. What do you do?
choices: Use the one you found first
pool.hint: How can you find out which one is right?
pool.explain: When sources disagree, a third trusted source helps you see which fact holds up.

pool.prompt: What should go in your list of sources?
choices: The title and who made each source
pool.hint: Someone else should be able to find the same source.
pool.explain: Give the title and who made each source, books and websites alike, so a reader can find and check it.

pool.prompt: You checked {n} facts in two sources. {k} of them needed a third source because the first two disagreed. How many facts did the two sources agree on?
pool.hint: Take away the facts that needed more checking.

pool.prompt: Your list of sources has {p} print sources and {d} digital sources. How many sources are on the list?
pool.hint: Add the print and the digital sources.
pool.explain: {p} print + {d} digital = {=p+d} sources on the list.

pool.prompt: You have the note 'ground swells up before eruptions'. Which question does it answer?
choices: What warns people that a volcano may erupt?
pool.hint: Is the note about a place, a size or a sign?
pool.explain: Swelling ground is a warning sign, so the note goes under the warning question.
